html:
The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children taken from their families by Australian governments and churches, mostly between about 1910 and 1970.

Laws in every state and territory let officials remove Indigenous children, above all those of mixed descent, without a court order. The aim was to absorb them into white society and, in the words of some officials, let Aboriginal people "die out". Children were put in missions, government homes and white foster families, often far away, sometimes with new names and told their parents were dead. Many were used as unpaid servants and farm hands.

Official estimates say that in some regions between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children were taken. The loss of language, culture and family echoed through later generations of Aboriginal Australians.

The 1997 report Bringing Them Home brought the story to national attention. On 13 February 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd made a formal apology in parliament. The removals sit beside the 1967 referendum and the Mabo case in the long story of Indigenous rights in Australia.
sum: The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children taken from their families by Australian governments and churches, mostly between about 1910 and 1970.
